entry.title: Yale’s 14 October broad U.S. tracker update still finds no clear AI labor-market footprint in its visible summary. It does not rule out narrower hiring changes.

A Swedish matched-hire study finds a 5–6% AI-skill pay gap versus occupational peers, but no remaining gap within the same firm; it does not measure a return to chatbot training or AI-caused job loss.
An Argentine randomized task test found a narrower education-based performance gap with AI access; it did not measure hiring, wages or job loss.
A U.S. worker survey finds widespread but often shallow generative AI task use; it measures adoption, not job losses or wages.
A U.S. STEM PhD study links detected AI writing with different post-degree career paths; the association does not show AI caused lost jobs.
A U.S. sector study finds higher relative employment where AI could assist tasks through 2024, but it measures exposure rather than employer use and does not settle AI-caused job loss.

Checked a German AI-skill-ad study’s 2026 journal version against its 2024 draft and a U.S. AI-use study. No new job-loss verdict: the German abstract reports no employment-growth link in its 2015–2023 window.

Added a conditional vulnerability estimate: 6.1 million U.S. workers in high-exposure occupations have low average transition capacity, but the study observes no AI-caused layoffs or reemployment outcomes.

Added opposing Copilot hiring signals: a conference estimate of fewer technical hires after induced adoption and a journal association with higher monthly incidence of software-engineer hiring. They count different outcomes and do not settle net jobs.
A randomized U.S. survey shows that a strong warning about student AI use lowered hiring professionals’ ratings of hypothetical graduates; it measured neither actual hires nor wages.
A London matched-application experiment found a pooled interview-invitation lift from an AI-related certificate for underrepresented women, but not parity, hiring or wage gains.
Danish firms first reporting AI use showed slower hiring relative to trend, mainly at small firms; this is an observational gap, not a layoff count.
A Danish study found no extra early-career-share decline at workplaces encouraging chatbots through 2024; it is the same underlying study already tracked, not a new replication.
A Federal Reserve manufacturing note finds broad AI skills in ads and a large unadjusted posted-pay gap; it does not show worker raises, hires or layoffs.
Added full-paper evidence that U.S. vacancy exposure changed through both the mix of posted roles and listed tasks within comparable groups; this is not an AI-caused job-loss estimate.

A U.S. startup study reports that more entry offset jobs lost at exposed incumbents without raising aggregate startup employment; a UK entry null narrows generalization of the prior startup-growth signal.
Added a CEPR startup-entry counter-signal: more entry and reported industry-level labor growth in more GenAI-exposed industries, with causal and coverage limits explicit.
Added a Census validation: exposure scores predict reported firm AI use only partly, so exposure-based job warnings are not proof of employer adoption or AI-caused losses.
Added a U.S. software-vacancy study: junior ads fell roughly 14–15% relative to senior ads after ChatGPT, but the study does not establish AI-caused hires or job losses.
Added a methodological test: platform conversation shares can change U.S. employment coefficients even when the labor-market design is fixed. This does not estimate AI-caused job loss.
